questions.question: Which property defines a continuous random variable in this course?
options: It can take only finitely many isolated values
It must have a probability mass function giving positive mass to each value
A nonnegative density $f_X$ whose integrals give interval probabilities
It is always normally distributed

questions.question: For a continuous random variable, how are probabilities usually assigned?
options: To single exact values with positive mass
Only to integers
To intervals of values
Only to outcomes named success and failure

questions.question: What is $P(X=c)$ for a continuous random variable and a fixed real number $c$?
What must be true about the function $f_X$ for a continuous random variable?
options: It must be negative somewhere
It must be a probability mass function
It must be nonnegative
It must integrate to a value greater than one

questions.question: What can be said about the CDF of a continuous random variable?
options: It must be a step function
It is always constant
It is continuous
It is undefined outside the support

questions.question: Which example is naturally modeled as a continuous random variable?
options: The number of heads in ten coin tosses
The number of aces in a five-card hand
The number of calls arriving in a minute
The lifetime of a light bulb

questions.question: The exact arrival time of a bus during an hour is best treated as what kind of variable?
options: A continuous random variable
A Bernoulli random variable
A hypergeometric random variable
A deterministic integer count

questions.question: If $X$ is continuous, which expression represents $P(2\le X\le 5)$?
options: $\int_2^5 f_X(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$
$5-2$ without using a density

questions.question: If scale measurement error is modeled continuously, what is the probability of exactly $0.100000$ error?
options: The density value at $0.100000$
The length of the measurement interval

questions.question: Which question is most appropriate for a continuous random variable?
options: What is the probability mass at each integer?
What is the probability that $X$ lies between $a$ and $b$?
Which draw is the first success?
How many objects are successes in a finite sample without replacement?

questions.question: Why do endpoints usually not matter for intervals of a continuous random variable?
options: Because densities are always zero at endpoints
Because all intervals have probability one
Because continuous variables cannot have endpoints
Because individual points have probability zero

questions.question: Why is a density value $f_X(c)$ not itself the probability $P(X=c)$?
options: The density is always an integer count
Point probabilities are zero; probabilities come from areas over intervals
The density value $f_X(c)$ must always be less than one, which confuses density with probability
$P(X=c)$ is always equal to one, which is false since point probabilities vanish

questions.question: Does a continuous random variable require its density to be continuous everywhere?
options: Yes, both CDF and density must be continuous everywhere, in all instances without exception.
No, its CDF is continuous but the density need not be continuous everywhere
No, because the CDF must have jumps
Yes, because every density is constant

questions.question: If $f_X(x)=1/4$ on $[0,4]$, what is $P(1\le X\le 3)$?
If $X$ is continuous, which equality is correct?
options: $P(1<X<2)=0$ for every density

questions.question: Which model choice is more appropriate for exact bus arrival time over a fixed window?
options: A hypergeometric variable counting successes
A geometric variable counting trials until success
A continuous random variable with interval probabilities
A Bernoulli variable with only two values

questions.question: Why does $P(X=c)=0$ not mean that the value $c$ is impossible in a continuous model?
options: The model secretly assigns positive mass to every point
The density must be zero everywhere
Probability is spread over uncountably many possible exact values
The CDF is undefined at $c$

questions.question: A continuous variable gives zero probability to each single point yet positive probability to intervals. Which role does the integral play?
options: It counts the number of isolated outcomes
It orders the sample space outcomes
It converts every variable into a Bernoulli variable
It accumulates density over an interval to produce probability

questions.question: A student says a continuous variable can have $P(X=2)=0.05$. What is the problem?
options: The value $2$ cannot lie in any interval, universally and without exception.
The probability must be at least $0.5$
A continuous random variable assigns probability zero to each exact value
The CDF must be negative at $2$

questions.question: If $P(0\le X\le 1)=0.3$ for continuous $X$, what is $P(0<X<1)$?
options: Less than $0.3$ by the probability of both endpoints
